title: Annexation, 1849
hook: after two wars with the British, Punjab is annexed and the boy king Duleep Singh sent to England

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and your line, the golden temple. Did something plain shine for a moment? Today, what happened to his kingdom, and to his youngest son. Then a look back at the week. Day two hundred ninety-four.

Picture a ten-year-old boy on a throne too big for him. He's the king, officially. His mother has been taken away from him. Grown men argue over his head in languages he half understands. And one spring day in 1849, he's asked to sign a paper that gives away his kingdom, and a diamond famous across the world. A few years later, he'll be living in England, thousands of miles from Punjab. Today: annexation, and the boy king Duleep Singh.
screen: `A TEN-YEAR-OLD ON A THRONE.` → `A PAPER TO SIGN, 1849.` → `THOUSANDS OF MILES FROM PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: After Ranjit Singh died in 1839, his kingdom fell into a decade of turmoil: rulers came and went, and several were killed. The British East India Company, already ruling much of India, was watching. Two wars followed between the Sikh kingdom and the British, in 1845 and 1848. The Sikh armies fought hard; some battles were among the fiercest the British had faced in India. But the kingdom lost. In March 1849, Punjab was annexed, taken into British India. The last Maharaja, Duleep Singh, Ranjit Singh's youngest son, was about ten. He was separated from his mother, Maharani Jind Kaur, placed with a British guardian, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond was sent to Queen Victoria. As a young teenager he became a Christian, and at fifteen he was taken to England, where he lived the life of a country gentleman. But in his forties, after meeting his mother again, he tried to return to Punjab and took up his Sikh faith once more. He was stopped on the way, and he died in Paris in 1893, far from home. Sikhs remember him with a particular ache, as the king who lost his home, his mother and his kingdom as a child. Now the week. The Chhota Ghallughara: remembered. Gurmata: decide together. Baba Deep Singh: finish the vow. The Vadda Ghallughara: the panth rose again. The misls: twelve, and one. Ranjit Singh: the golden temple. And annexation: far from home.
screen: `AFTER 1839, A DECADE OF TURMOIL.` · `TWO WARS; PUNJAB ANNEXED, 1849.` · `DULEEP SINGH, THE BOY KING.` · `A WEEK FROM LOSS TO GOLD TO EXILE.` · then, large: `FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who's far from home right now. A friend who moved abroad, a grandparent who left their village long ago, a student in a new city, a soldier, a refugee you've read about. Picture them where they are this evening. What might they miss most: a food, a language, a face, a sound? Hold them there for a few breaths with kindness. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Annexation. In 1849, after two wars, Punjab was taken into British India, and the boy king Duleep Singh was later sent to England, far from home.
Your line: far from home. Today, send a short message to someone living far from home. Day two hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the annexation of 1849 as the end of the Sikh kingdom; Maharaja Duleep Singh's story is widely told in the Sikh diaspora, especially in Britain, where a statue of him stands in Thetford, Norfolk.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Punjab, from Persian panj (five) and aab (waters): the land of five rivers.

trapdoor: what you thought: the British took over Punjab.
what it means: after two hard wars the Sikh kingdom ended, and its boy king lost his mother, his throne and his home.

what a scholar hears: Anglo-Sikh wars of 1845–46 and 1848–49; annexation proclaimed 29 March 1849; the Koh-i-Noor ceded under the Treaty of Lahore; Duleep Singh returned to Sikhism in 1886 and died in Paris in 1893.
